title: What is RAL Classic? Industrial Color Standard
summary: Learn how the RAL Classic color system works, its numbering ranges, common industrial color codes, and why standardizing RAL values matters for product catalogs.
body_markdown:
RAL Classic is a standardized color matching system used across European industrial manufacturing. It defines approximately 215 colors, each identified by a four-digit code (e.g., RAL 7035 for light grey). It is the dominant color specification method for enclosures, cable trays, switchgear housings, and other electrical products in Europe.


## History and purpose


The RAL color system was created in 1927 by the Reichsausschuss fur Lieferbedingungen (RAL, or the National Committee for Delivery Conditions) in Germany. The original motivation was straightforward: when a manufacturer and a customer agreed on a color, they needed a shared reference that did not depend on subjective description or physical samples that could fade.


The first RAL color table had 40 colors. Today, RAL Classic contains approximately 215 standardized colors. Each has a four-digit code, a German name, and translations in multiple languages. The system is maintained by RAL gGmbH, a subsidiary of the RAL Deutsches Institut fur Gutesicherung und Kennzeichnung.


RAL Classic is not the only RAL system. RAL Design (introduced 1993) uses seven-digit codes based on CIELAB color space, and RAL Effect (introduced 2007) adds metallic and solid colors. But RAL Classic remains the standard referenced in electrical product specifications, DIN standards, and industrial procurement.


## How the numbering works


RAL Classic codes follow a four-digit structure where the first digit indicates the color range:


First digit Color range Example


1 Yellow tones RAL 1003 Signal yellow


2 Orange tones RAL 2004 Pure orange


3 Red tones RAL 3000 Flame red


4 Violet tones RAL 4001 Red lilac


5 Blue tones RAL 5010 Gentian blue


6 Green tones RAL 6005 Moss green


7 Grey tones RAL 7035 Light grey


8 Brown tones RAL 8014 Sepia brown


9 Black and white tones RAL 9010 Pure white


Within each range, the remaining three digits identify the specific shade. The numbers are not sequential. RAL 7001 (silver grey), RAL 7016 (anthracite grey), RAL 7035 (light grey), and RAL 7040 (window grey) are all in the grey range, but there are gaps in the numbering because not every possible three-digit combination is assigned.


## Colors that matter in electrical distribution


If you work with electrical product catalogs, you will see the same RAL codes repeatedly. Here are the most common:


### Enclosures and cabinets


RAL Code Color name Typical application


RAL 7035 Light grey Standard enclosure color (Rittal, ABB, Schneider)


RAL 7032 Pebble grey Older enclosure standard, still common


RAL 7016 Anthracite grey Premium and IT enclosures


RAL 7021 Black grey Server racks, data center enclosures


RAL 9005 Jet black High-end enclosures, architectural


RAL 9010 Pure white Clean room and food industry enclosures


RAL 7035 is by far the most specified color in the electrical enclosure market. Rittal, the world's largest enclosure manufacturer, uses it as the default for nearly their entire steel enclosure range. When a spec sheet says "standard color" for an enclosure, it almost always means RAL 7035.


### Cable management


RAL Code Color name Typical application


RAL 7035 Light grey Cable trays, trunking systems


RAL 7030 Stone grey Cable ducts


RAL 9001 Cream PVC trunking


RAL 9010 Pure white Surface-mount cable channels


### Safety and signaling


RAL Code Color name Typical application


RAL 1003 Signal yellow Warning markings, safety barriers


RAL 3000 Flame red Fire alarm devices, emergency stops


RAL 3001 Signal red Fire safety equipment


RAL 6024 Traffic green Emergency exit signs


RAL 5015 Sky blue Mandatory action signs


## RAL Classic vs other color systems


### RAL vs Hex/RGB


RAL colors do not map one-to-one to hex or RGB values. A RAL color is a physical standard defined by spectrophotometric measurements. The hex approximations you find online are screen representations that vary by monitor calibration. RAL 7035 is commonly approximated as #C5C7C4 or #D7D7D7 depending on the source. Neither is authoritative.


For product data purposes: store the RAL code, not a hex approximation. The RAL code is the specification. The hex value is a display convenience.


### RAL vs NCS


The Natural Color System (NCS) is used primarily in Scandinavia and for architectural applications. It uses a different notation (e.g., NCS S 1502-Y for a color similar to RAL 7035). Some Scandinavian electrical suppliers reference NCS codes alongside RAL. If you encounter both, store both.


### RAL vs Pantone


Pantone is dominant in print and branding but rarely used for industrial products. You will occasionally see Pantone references on product packaging or marketing materials, but the technical specification for the product color is almost always RAL.


## Why RAL matters for product data


Color is a filterable attribute. When a contractor searches your webshop for "light grey enclosure," they expect to find enclosures in RAL 7035. If your catalog stores color as free text ("light grey," "lichtgrau," "gris clair," "gray"), the search works poorly and cross-supplier comparison is impossible.


Standardizing on RAL codes solves this. RAL 7035 is RAL 7035 regardless of language. It enables faceted search, cross-supplier comparison, and automated matching between the color a specifier requests and the color a manufacturer offers.

## Common data quality issues with RAL codes


**Inconsistent formatting.** The same color appears as "RAL7035," "RAL 7035," "7035," "ral-7035," or "RAL-7035" across different supplier feeds. Your system should normalize all of these to a canonical format.


**Invalid codes.** Not every four-digit number starting with 1-9 is a valid RAL Classic code. RAL 7099 does not exist. Typos and fabricated codes enter your catalog when data is manually entered.


**Confusing RAL Classic with RAL Design.** A seven-digit code like "RAL 210 50 35" is a RAL Design code, not RAL Classic. They are different systems. If a supplier sends a seven-digit RAL code, do not truncate it to four digits.


**Missing color data.** Many suppliers do not include RAL codes in their data feeds even when the product has a defined RAL color. This forces distributors to look up colors from PDF spec sheets or physical catalogs and enter them manually, which is where most errors originate.
